\chapter{Five Things You Ask For --- Soap, Towel, Glass, Spoon, Plate}
\label{ch:cinco-cosas}
\hlchaptermodality{287}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for soap, a towel, a glass, a spoon and a plate in Spanish, politely.}

Complete ES-C287-plato: ask for all five in turn, with por favor on the end of each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el jabón]{el jabón — a word that went abroad and came home}

\label{lesson:ES-C287-jabon}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: how many times did English borrow \emph{febris}? (Twice.) And what does \emph{dolere} mean? (To hurt.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el agua — what you use this with.
  \item por favor — what you put on the end when you ask.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ja-BON}, stress on the second syllable, which the written accent marks. The \emph{j} is the \emph{jota} again, the rasp at the back. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el jabón} — \textquotedblleft{}soap.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{sapo}, \textbf{saponem} — and Latin did not make this word. It borrowed it from the Germanic peoples on its northern frontier, who used the stuff on their hair before anybody in Rome used it for washing.

So English \textbf{soap} and \emph{jabón} are one word, and the English one is the one that stayed at home. Spanish has it back after a long detour: Germanic into Latin, Latin into Spanish. \textbf{Saponify} and \textbf{saponification} are the late loans, taken straight from the Latin form.

Words move with things. Rome had better roads and better law; the north had better soap. Trade decides vocabulary far more often than conquest does.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Not every Latin word is Roman.

Latin was borrowing from its neighbours the whole time, and a word can be perfectly good Latin and still be an import. \emph{Jabón} has been abroad and come back, and nothing in the sound of it says so.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el jabón}
  \item \emph{el jabón, por favor}
  \item \emph{jabón} and \emph{soap}, and hear one word twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where did Latin get \emph{sapo}? (From its Germanic neighbours.) Is English \emph{soap} borrowed from Spanish? (No — it never left; it is the same word at home.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la toalla]{la toalla — the Germanic layer, still in the bathroom}

\label{lesson:ES-C287-toalla}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: where did Latin get \emph{sapo}? (From its Germanic neighbours.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el jabón — what you use before you need this.
  \item el agua — and what you are drying off.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{to-A-lla}, stress on the \emph{a}. The \emph{ll} is a \emph{y} sound for most speakers, and something closer to a \emph{j} in the River Plate. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la toalla} — \textquotedblleft{}a towel.\textquotedblright{}

Another Germanic word, and this time both languages took it. Frankish \textbf{thwahlja}, a cloth for washing, became Old French \emph{toaille}, and out of that Spanish has \emph{toalla} and English has \textbf{towel}.

Two words in a row now that are not Latin at the bottom. Spanish is a Latin language with a Germanic layer laid over the top, and that layer sits mostly in the house and the wardrobe — the words the settlers brought along with the things themselves.

The \emph{-alla} ending is the giveaway. A Latin word would not have arrived in that shape; a French one would. Spanish borrowed this from its neighbour, not from its parent.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two Germanic words, side by side, in the plainest room of the house.

That is not an accident. The most domestic vocabulary in a Romance language is often the least Roman, because that is where the incomers actually lived.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la toalla}
  \item \emph{la toalla, por favor}
  \item \emph{el jabón y la toalla}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \emph{toalla} a Latin word? (No — Frankish, through French.) Which English word is the same one? (\emph{Towel}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el vaso]{el vaso — named for the job, not the material}

\label{lesson:ES-C287-vaso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: is \emph{toalla} a Latin word? (No — Frankish, through French.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el agua — what goes in it.
  \item la toalla — the thing before this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{VA-so}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{v} is the same soft sound as \emph{b} — the letters differ and the sound does not. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el vaso} — \textquotedblleft{}a glass,\textquotedblright{} the thing you drink out of.

Latin \textbf{vas}, \textbf{vasis}: a vessel, a container of any sort. Spanish names the object by what it does rather than by what it is made of, which is why a plastic one is still a \emph{vaso} and an English glass made of plastic is a small embarrassment.

English has three of them at three different weights. A \textbf{vase} holds flowers. A \textbf{vessel} holds wine, or cargo, or blood. The \textbf{vascular} system is the body's plumbing, named by anatomists reaching for the same Latin.

And notice the letter. \emph{Vaso} begins with the sound you have been giving to \emph{b}. Spanish writes \emph{v} and says something very close to \emph{b}, and that was true long before the spelling settled down.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three things you can ask for, and three different sources.

Germanic, Frankish, Latin. A tray of ordinary objects in a Spanish kitchen is a small map of who passed through.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el vaso}
  \item \emph{un vaso de agua, por favor}
  \item \emph{vaso} and \emph{vase}, and hear the container in both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{vas} mean in Latin? (A vessel or container.) Why is a plastic one still a \emph{vaso}? (Because the word names the job, not the material.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la cuchara]{la cuchara — a snail shell with a handle}

\label{lesson:ES-C287-cuchara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vas} mean in Latin? (A vessel.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el vaso — the thing before this one.
  \item la comida — what you need this for.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cu-CHA-ra}, stress in the middle. The \emph{ch} is one sound, as in English \emph{church}, and never a \emph{k}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cuchara} — \textquotedblleft{}a spoon.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{cochlear}, a spoon, from \textbf{cochlea}, a snail shell. The Romans ate snails and used the shell to get them out, and the tool kept the name of the shell long after it had stopped being one.

\textbf{Cochlea} is still in English, unchanged, for the spiral inside your ear — named by an anatomist who thought it looked like the shell. So the spoon and the inner ear are the same Latin snail, arriving a thousand years apart by two completely different routes.

A tool named after the thing it replaced is one of the commonest patterns in any vocabulary. The name outlives the object, and nobody notices until somebody pulls the word open.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four things, and each one is a small piece of history you can hold.

Soap from the north, a towel from the Franks, a vessel from Rome, and a snail shell with a handle on it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cuchara}
  \item \emph{la cuchara, por favor}
  \item \emph{cochlea} and \emph{cuchara}, the shell and the spoon
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{cochlea}? (A snail shell.) What else in English carries the name? (The spiral of the inner ear.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el plato]{el plato — flat, in Greek, before anything else}

\label{lesson:ES-C287-plato}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what is a \emph{cochlea}? (A snail shell.) And what did \emph{vas} mean? (A vessel.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cuchara — what you put beside it.
  \item por favor — what closes every one of these requests.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PLA-to}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{l} stays clear and forward, and the \emph{pl} is said cleanly with no vowel slipped in. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el plato} — \textquotedblleft{}a plate.\textquotedblright{}

Not Latin at the bottom: Greek \textbf{platys}, flat or broad. Latin took it in as \emph{plattus}, and out of that Spanish has \emph{plato} and English has \textbf{plate}.

The same Greek flatness turns up all over. A \textbf{plaza} is a flat open space — Latin \emph{platea}, a broad street. A \textbf{plateau} is a flat high place. A \textbf{platypus} is a flat-foot. And English \textbf{flat} itself is the Germanic cousin of \emph{platys}, from the same ancient root by the other road.

Five things you can now ask for. The asking itself you have had for a long while: \emph{por favor} on the end of any of them, and the sentence is finished.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{el jabón}, \emph{la toalla}, \emph{el vaso}, \emph{la cuchara}, \emph{el plato}.

Germanic, Frankish, Latin, Latin, Greek. Five ordinary objects and five different origins — which is the honest answer to the question of where Spanish words come from.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el plato}
  \item \emph{el plato, por favor}
  \item all five in order — \emph{el jabón}, \emph{la toalla}, \emph{el vaso}, \emph{la cuchara}, \emph{el plato}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{platys} mean? (Flat.) What is a \emph{platypus}, taken apart? (A flat-foot.) And where did Latin get \emph{sapo}? (From its Germanic neighbours.)
\end{tcolorbox}
